o:
nums[i] * nums[a] is a perfect square exactly when nums[i] and nums[a] have the same squarefree part (product of primes appearing to an odd power). So reduce every value to its squarefree kernel, and the question becomes: for each node, how many ancestors share its kernel? Doing a DFS from the root while maintaining a counter of kernels on the current root-to-node path answers this directly: when entering a node, add the current count of its kernel to the answer, then insert it; when leaving, remove it.

Example 1: kernels of [2,8,2] are [2,2,2]; node 1 sees one prior 2, node 2 sees two, total 3. Values up to 1e5 mean kernels can be precomputed for all numbers with a smallest-prime-factor sieve.
k: x*y is a perfect square iff squarefree(x) == squarefree(y)
DFS with a global counter map, incremented on entry and decremented on exit, counts ancestors with matching kernel per path
Precompute squarefree kernels for 1..1e5 with an SPF sieve in O(V log V)

a.n: Approach 1: DFS with Path Kernel Counter
a.i: Root the tree at 0. Maintain a hash map from kernel value to count of nodes currently on the DFS path. At each node, first add the existing count of its own kernel to the answer (those are exactly its ancestors with matching kernel), then record itself, recurse, and undo on exit.
s: Sieve smallest prime factors up to 1e5; compute kernel(v) for every nums[i]
Iterative DFS from root; on entry: ans += count[kernel[u]], count[kernel[u]]++; push an exit marker
a.t: O(V log V + n α) — SPF sieve plus linear DFS with O(1) hash operations per node
a.sp: O(V + n) — sieve, adjacency list, counter map, and explicit stack

w: This DFS-with-undo pattern is the standard tool for 'statistics over ancestors' problems. Alternatives (Euler tour + offline BIT per kernel) exist but add complexity without changing asymptotics. Pitfalls: computing the kernel incorrectly (track exponent parity, not just distinct primes), recursion depth on a 1e5-deep path (use an explicit stack in Python/JS), and answering the node itself — the count must be read before inserting the node's own kernel. Follow-up: handle node updates with Heavy-Light decomposition or Euler-tour BITs.
